meta.title: Automation, agents and data
meta.description: n8n, agent skills and the agent harness, PostgreSQL and SQLite as databases and vector stores. Facts checked on 2026-10-19; texts and ratings are proposals.

facts.text: The Docker image is n8nio/n8n. Its data lives in /home/node/.n8n and the web interface is on port 5678.
Docker Compose is the route for production. npm is meant for local testing and is deprecated from n8n 3.0.
The npm install needs Node.js 20.19 up to 24.x.
SQLite is the default database. PostgreSQL is supported by setting DB_TYPE=postgresdb.
Supported PostgreSQL versions are the latest two (17 and 18 as of July 2026) plus 16.
The MCP Server Trigger documents SSE and streamable HTTP.
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md. It needs a name (up to 64 characters, lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, same as the folder) and a description (up to 1,024 characters).
A skill can add scripts/, references/ and assets/ folders.
Skills load in three steps: name and description first, then the full instructions, then files on demand.
Many products support skills, but the agent decides whether to use a skill it found.
Claude Code reads skills from .claude/skills/ or ~/.claude/skills/.
VS Code reads skills from .github/skills/, .claude/skills/ and .agents/skills/.
Subagents live in .claude/agents/ in Claude Code.
Dynamic workflows run up to 16 agents at once and up to 1,000 per run.
CLAUDE.md is the instruction file in Claude Code. AGENTS.md can be read in its place.
MCP connects an agent to tools and data through one open standard.
PostgreSQL 18 is current (18.6) and supported until 2030-11-14.
PostgreSQL 14 reaches end of life on 2026-11-12.
An official Docker image exists. For version 18 its data volume is /var/lib/postgresql.
pgvector 0.8.7 works with PostgreSQL 13 and later. It adds the types vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec, and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes.
Enable pgvector with CREATE EXTENSION vector; in each database that uses it.
SQLite 3.54.1 was released on 2026-10-16.
SQLite is an in-process library that stores everything in one file. It is in the public domain.
Loading extensions is off by default.
FTS5 full-text search is not enabled in every build.
sqlite-vec is pre-v1, so breaking changes are possible. It uses vec0 virtual tables.
sqlite-vec has bindings for Python, Node.js, Ruby, Go and Rust, under Apache-2.0 and MIT.

openPoints.text: The n8n documentation lists no base URL field for the OpenAI credential. A maintainer reply says custom base URLs already work.
openPoints.owner: Check the credential form in your n8n version

openPoints.text: The MCP Client Tool page documents only an SSE endpoint. Check again before relying on streamable HTTP in the client.
openPoints.owner: n8n documentation and the n8n version in use

openPoints.text: Not checked: whether the embeddings sub-nodes work with your own model endpoint.
Status values and difficulty ratings are proposals.
Subagent, dynamic workflow and hook details come from Claude Code documentation only.
openPoints.owner: Check the documentation of the harness you use

openPoints.text: GitHub Copilot was verified for skills only.
openPoints.owner: Check the Copilot documentation if this profile should cover it

openPoints.text: PostgreSQL retires its oldest major version each November. Re-check version numbers and the range n8n supports before each release.
Check that the SQLite build you use allows loading extensions before relying on sqlite-vec.

platforms.label: Docker
platforms.summary: Container runtime for ready-made images such as n8n and PostgreSQL.
platforms.why: A container packs a tool with everything it needs, so the machine only needs Docker and no tool-by-tool installation.
platforms.what: Docker Desktop for Mac, Windows and Linux includes Docker Engine and Docker Compose. On Linux, Engine and Compose can also be installed on their own, which suits machines without a graphical desktop.
how: Install Docker Desktop, or Docker Engine and Compose on a Linux server.
Create volumes for the data that must survive restarts.
Start the image with its ports and volumes, or use a Compose file.

installation.why: A standard installer. Linux servers use separate Engine and Compose packages.

usage.why: Images, volumes, ports and updates need some container knowledge.

platforms.label: Node.js
platforms.summary: JavaScript runtime for MCP servers, scripts and npm-installed tools.
platforms.why: Many AI tools start through Node.js (npx or npm), so the runtime has to be there first.
platforms.what: A JavaScript runtime that runs outside the browser. Every tool states its own version need. n8n installed with npm needs 20.19 up to 24.x.
how: Install a Node.js version that your tools support.
Check it in a terminal with node --version.

installation.why: An installer is enough, but versions must match what the tools expect.

usage.why: Runs in the background. Nobody has to use it directly.

platforms.label: Python
platforms.summary: Runtime for skill scripts and MCP servers built with the Python SDK.
platforms.why: Skill scripts and many MCP servers are written in Python, so the interpreter and its packages must exist on the machine.
platforms.what: A programming language runtime. Skill scripts and MCP servers written with the official Python SDK run on it.
how: Install a Python version that your scripts support.
Install the packages a script needs, ideally in a virtual environment.

installation.why: An installer is enough, but packages and versions differ per script.

usage.why: Runs in the background. Nobody has to use it directly.

platforms.label: VS Code
platforms.summary: Code editor that hosts Copilot, Claude Code and other agent extensions.
platforms.why: Editor-based agents do not run on their own. Everyone who uses them needs the editor.
platforms.what: Microsoft's code editor. Extensions such as GitHub Copilot and the Claude Code extension run inside it.
how: Install VS Code from the company software portal or the official download page.
Open it and sign in to the extensions you need.

installation.why: A standard installer, usually already present on developer machines.

usage.why: Familiar to developers, new for everyone else.

bricks.name: n8n
bricks.summary: Low-code workflow editor with AI agent nodes, hosted as a container or Node.js app.
bricks.why: Teams build automations and AI agents by connecting nodes in a visual editor instead of writing code. One tool joins model endpoints, databases and MCP servers.
bricks.what: A workflow platform you host yourself. Its AI Agent node connects a chat model with tools. It can call external MCP servers (MCP Client Tool) and offer its own tools as an MCP server (MCP Server Trigger). It stores workflows, credentials and runs in SQLite by default, or in PostgreSQL. Docker Compose is the documented route for production. npm installs are for local tests and deprecated from n8n 3.0.
how: Install Docker (Docker Desktop, or Docker Engine and Compose on a Linux server).
Create a data volume and start the n8nio/n8n image on port 5678 with the volume mounted at /home/node/.n8n. For production use the Docker Compose setup.
Open http://localhost:5678 and finish the first-time setup.
Add credentials for your model endpoint and databases, then build a workflow with the AI Agent node.

installation.why: Docker, a persistent volume and ports are set up by hand. Production adds Compose, a PostgreSQL database and regular updates (new minor versions most weeks).

usage.why: The editor is visual, but agents, credentials, expressions and tool wiring take practice.

bricks.name: OpenAI-compatible endpoint
bricks.summary: A language-model service that answers in the OpenAI API format.
bricks.why: One tool can talk to many model providers or to a local model server, because they share the same request format.
bricks.what: Any hosted or self-run service that offers an OpenAI-style HTTP API. It needs a base URL and usually an API key. n8n reaches it through its OpenAI credential and the OpenAI Chat Model node, which uses the Chat Completions format unless Use Responses API is switched on.
how: Choose a provider, or start a local model server that offers an OpenAI-style API.
Note its base URL and, if required, create an API key.
Create an OpenAI credential in n8n and look for a base URL field in your version.
Select the model in the OpenAI Chat Model node of your workflow.

installation.why: An account, key and base URL must be arranged. A local model server also has to be hosted.

usage.why: Choose a model in a node. Providers differ in what they support.

bricks.name: MCP server
bricks.summary: A program that offers tools and data to AI applications over MCP.
bricks.why: Connects your own systems to an AI agent through one open standard, so each system is wired up once and works in many agents.
bricks.what: MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to outside systems. An MCP server offers tools, data or prompts. In n8n, the MCP Client Tool node documents an SSE endpoint with bearer, header or OAuth2 authentication.
how: Pick a ready-made server or build one with the official SDK (Node.js or Python).
Start it, or note its endpoint URL if it runs remotely.
Register it in the MCP settings of your client and set the authentication.
Choose which of its tools the agent may use.

installation.why: The entry is added by hand to each client, and the server needs Node.js or Python or a remote endpoint.

usage.why: Once registered, the agent calls the tools by itself. The results still need review.

bricks.name: PostgreSQL
bricks.summary: Open-source relational database server that also takes extensions such as pgvector.
bricks.why: Holds structured business data and, with the pgvector extension, the embeddings for semantic search in one reliable system that many tools already support.
bricks.what: A database server with SQL and a catalogue of extensions. PostgreSQL 18 is the current major version (18.6 on 2026-10-19). Each major version is supported for five years. Installers and packages exist for Linux, macOS, Windows and BSD, and there is an official Docker image.
how: Pick a supported major version. 18 is current, so check the versioning page.
Install it from the packages or installer for your OS, or start the official postgres Docker image with POSTGRES_PASSWORD set and a data volume (for 18 the image volume is /var/lib/postgresql).
Create a database and a user for your application.
Connect your tool with host, port, database and credentials.

installation.why: A server to install, secure and update. In Docker, volumes and the password variable must be right.

usage.why: SQL plus users, backups and upgrades need database know-how.

bricks.name: SQLite
bricks.summary: Serverless SQL database in a single file, built into many tools.
bricks.why: Needs no server and no setup, so apps, scripts and agents can keep structured data in one portable file.
bricks.what: A C library that runs inside the application and reads and writes an ordinary file, with ACID transactions. Public domain. Latest release 3.54.1 (2026-10-16). Full-text search (FTS5) is part of the source but not enabled in every build. Vector search needs an extension such as sqlite-vec. n8n uses SQLite by default for its own data.
how: Check whether your tool or language already bundles SQLite. Python does.
Otherwise download the library or the command-line shell from sqlite.org.
Open or create a database file. It is created on first use.
Add extensions when needed. Loading is off by default and the application must switch it on.

installation.why: Usually already present, and there is no server to run.

usage.why: Plain SQL. Extensions need an extra step.

bricks.name: pgvector
bricks.summary: PostgreSQL extension that stores embeddings and finds similar ones.
bricks.why: Adds semantic search to a database you already run. Documents and their vectors stay together, and no separate vector database is needed.
bricks.what: An open-source extension (version 0.8.7) for PostgreSQL 13 and later. It adds the types vector, halfvec, bit and sparsevec, distance operators (L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming, Jaccard) and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes for approximate search. Exact search works without an index. A vector column can hold up to 16,000 dimensions, an HNSW index on type vector up to 2,000.
how: Install pgvector for your PostgreSQL version: packages, a Docker image such as pgvector/pgvector, or build from source.
Run CREATE EXTENSION vector; once in each database.
Create a table with a vector(N) column, where N is the size your embedding model produces.
Insert embeddings and search with ORDER BY embedding <-> '[...]' LIMIT 5. Add an HNSW or IVFFlat index for approximate search.

installation.why: Packages and Docker images exist, then one CREATE EXTENSION command per database.

usage.why: Embeddings must come from a model, and distance and index settings need some understanding.

bricks.name: Agent skill
bricks.summary: A folder with a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a repeatable task.
bricks.why: Packs team know-how into portable, version-controlled folders, so any compatible agent follows the same procedure without being told again.
bricks.what: An open format: a folder with a required SKILL.md (name, description, instructions) and optional scripts/, references/ and assets/ folders. The agent reads only name and description at startup, loads the full instructions when a task matches, and opens further files on demand. A skill is not an app. It needs an agent harness to run.
how: Create a folder named like the skill: lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 64 characters.
Write SKILL.md with name and description in the header. The description says what the skill does and when to use it (at most 1,024 characters).
Add scripts, references or assets and point to them from SKILL.md with relative paths.
Put the folder where your harness looks, for example .claude/skills/ in a project or ~/.claude/skills/ for yourself.
Optionally check the format with the skills-ref library.

installation.why: Copy a folder into a skills location. The locations differ per harness.

usage.why: The agent decides when to load it, and use is not guaranteed. Descriptions must be specific.

bricks.name: Skill script
bricks.summary: Executable code in the scripts folder of a skill.
bricks.why: Turns written instructions into repeatable, checkable actions, such as converting a file or calling an API, instead of letting the agent improvise each time.
bricks.what: A script that the agent runs. Python, Bash and JavaScript are common, and the supported languages depend on the harness. The script is executed and does not have to be loaded into the agent's context. It should be self-contained or document its dependencies and give helpful error messages.
how: Pick a language that the harness supports and the machine has.
Put the script in the skill's scripts/ folder and document its dependencies.
Reference it from SKILL.md and say when and how to run it.
Install the needed packages on every machine where the skill runs.

installation.why: Interpreter, packages and permission settings must be right on every machine.

usage.why: The agent runs it and people review the result.

bricks.name: Agent harness
bricks.summary: The program around the model: agent loop, tools, skills and permissions.
bricks.why: A model alone only answers. The harness lets it read files, run commands and use tools under permission control, and decides which skills, tools and instructions the agent sees.
bricks.what: Examples are Claude Code and GitHub Copilot in VS Code. A harness loads instructions, skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers, asks before it acts, and runs in a terminal, an IDE, a desktop app or the web. Component names differ between products. This entry follows the Claude Code and VS Code documentation.
how: Choose a harness your organisation allows, for example Claude Code or GitHub Copilot in VS Code.
Install it: Claude Code by native installer, Homebrew or WinGet, Copilot as a VS Code extension.
Sign in and open a project folder.
Add project instructions, skills and MCP servers.
Review each action the agent asks permission for until you trust the setup.

installation.why: A standard installer or extension plus a sign-in.

usage.why: Prompting, permission prompts and reviewing results take practice.

bricks.name: Instruction file
bricks.summary: A Markdown file that the agent reads at the start of every session.
bricks.why: Keeps team rules, architecture decisions and checklists in the repository, so every session starts with the same context.
bricks.what: CLAUDE.md in Claude Code. If a repository already has an AGENTS.md for other coding agents, Claude Code can read that instead. Typical content: coding standards, preferred libraries and review checklists.
how: Create the file in the project root.
List standards, commands and rules in plain language.
Commit it so the whole team shares it.

installation.why: A text file in the repository.

usage.why: Easy to write, but the agent may not follow every rule.

bricks.name: Subagent
bricks.summary: A helper agent with its own context window, tools and permissions.
bricks.why: Keeps long searches and logs out of the main conversation and splits a task among specialised workers.
bricks.what: In Claude Code, a Markdown file with a YAML header (name and description are required, the body is the system prompt) in .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/. Only its final summary returns to the main conversation. Subagents cannot start further subagents beyond a depth limit (three layers by default).
how: Create .claude/agents/<name>.md with name and description in the header.
Write the role and rules as the body.
Limit its tools with the tools field.
Call it by name or @-mention, or let the harness choose from the description.

installation.why: A Markdown file that the team can share through the repository.

usage.why: Needs careful descriptions and tool limits, and results come back as summaries.

bricks.name: Dynamic workflow
bricks.summary: A rerunnable script that orchestrates many subagents.
bricks.why: One request can fan out over hundreds of files or sources. The plan is held in code, so runs are repeatable and the main conversation stays small.
bricks.what: In Claude Code, a JavaScript script that Claude writes and a runtime executes in the background. A run can use dozens to hundreds of agents (up to 16 at once by default, 1,000 per run). A good run can be saved as a command in .claude/workflows/ or shipped in a plugin. One run can use far more tokens than a normal chat.
how: Describe the task and ask for a workflow, or run the bundled /deep-research command.
Approve the plan that Claude Code shows before the run starts.
Watch progress with /workflows. Pause or stop agents there.
Save a good run as a command with the s key in /workflows.

installation.why: Nothing to install, but on some plans the feature has to be switched on in the settings.

usage.why: Needs judgement about scale, cost and permissions, and the results need checking.

bricks.name: Hook
bricks.summary: A shell command that the harness runs before or after an action.
bricks.why: Enforces rules automatically, such as formatting after every edit or linting before a commit, whether or not the model remembers the rule.
bricks.what: In Claude Code, hooks run shell commands around actions such as file edits. A PreToolUse hook can also allow or block a tool call. They are configured in the settings, not in the prompt.
how: Decide which action to react to, for example after a file edit.
Add the hook with its command to the Claude Code settings.
Test it on a throw-away change.

installation.why: Shell commands must be wired to the right events in the settings.

usage.why: A wrong hook blocks or slows the agent, so it needs developer skill.

bricks.name: sqlite-vec
bricks.summary: SQLite extension that stores vectors and finds nearest neighbours.
bricks.why: Gives local, file-based apps semantic search without a separate vector database.
bricks.what: A small extension in pure C without dependencies, the successor of sqlite-vss, under Apache-2.0 and MIT. Float, int8 and binary vectors live in vec0 virtual tables. It is pre-v1, so breaking changes are possible. Bindings exist for Python, Node.js, Ruby, Go and Rust. It runs on Linux, macOS, Windows, in browsers via WASM and on Raspberry Pi.
how: Install the binding for your language or download a release build.
Enable extension loading in your application. SQLite has it off by default, the sqlite3 shell has it on.
Load the extension. In the shell: .load ./vec0
Create a vec0 virtual table, insert vectors, and query with MATCH and ORDER BY distance.

installation.why: The build must match the platform and be loaded by hand. Pre-v1, so versions should be pinned.

usage.why: Embeddings must come from a model, and the interface may still change.

recipes.title: AI agent workflow with MCP tools
recipes.why: An automation can let a language model decide which tools to call, so routine multi-step work needs no hand-written branching.
recipes.what: n8n's AI Agent node gets a chat model from the endpoint and calls the tools of an MCP server through the MCP Client Tool node.
how: Start n8n in Docker.
Create the credential for your model endpoint.
Add an AI Agent node with a chat model and an MCP Client Tool node that points to your MCP server.
Choose which tools the agent may use and run the workflow.
recipes.example: An agent reads a support mail, looks the customer up through an MCP server and drafts a reply.

installation.why: Docker, the credential and the MCP connection are all set up by hand the first time.

usage.why: Agent behaviour must be tested and the tool calls reviewed.

recipes.title: n8n with PostgreSQL storage
recipes.why: n8n keeps workflows, credentials and runs in SQLite by default. PostgreSQL is the documented alternative for setups that need more than a single file.
recipes.what: n8n is switched to PostgreSQL with DB_TYPE=postgresdb and the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables. The n8n data folder still has to be kept, for the encryption key and logs.
how: Start a PostgreSQL server or container with a database and user for n8n.
Set DB_TYPE=postgresdb and the DB_POSTGRESDB_* variables for the n8n container.
Keep the /home/node/.n8n volume.
Start n8n and check that it connects.
recipes.example: A Docker Compose file starts PostgreSQL and n8n side by side.

installation.why: Two services, their variables and two persistent volumes must fit together.

usage.why: After the setup nothing changes for the people who build workflows.

recipes.title: Question answering over your own documents
recipes.why: People get answers from their own documents without a separate vector database. The text and its vectors stay in a database the team already runs.
recipes.what: n8n's PGVector Vector Store node inserts documents into a Postgres table and searches them. A chat model from the endpoint writes the answer from the hits.
how: Run PostgreSQL and enable pgvector with CREATE EXTENSION vector;
Add a Postgres credential in n8n.
Build one workflow that inserts documents with the PGVector Vector Store node, and one agent workflow that searches it as a tool.
Ask a question and check the answer against the source documents.
recipes.example: Employees ask the agent about internal handbook rules and get answers taken from the handbook text.

installation.why: Several pieces must work together: PostgreSQL, the extension, an embeddings model, document loading and the n8n credentials.

usage.why: Quality depends on how documents are split and searched, which needs testing.

recipes.title: A skill with a bundled script
recipes.why: A written procedure plus a script gives the same result every time, because the agent runs tested code for the exact steps.
recipes.what: SKILL.md explains when and how to run the script. The agent loads the instructions when a task matches and then executes the script.
how: Write SKILL.md with a specific description.
Add the script under scripts/ and name its dependencies.
Install the interpreter and packages on each machine.
Ask for a task that matches the description and check that the skill is used.
recipes.example: A skill converts a folder of scans to text. The agent runs the bundled Python script and reports the files it processed.

installation.why: The interpreter, packages and the skills folder must be right on every machine.

usage.why: Describe the task. The script does the repeatable part.

recipes.title: A team procedure as a shared skill
recipes.why: A repeatable team procedure becomes something every developer's agent follows in the same way.
recipes.what: The harness lists the skill by name and description, loads SKILL.md when a task matches and runs the bundled script for the exact steps.
how: Write SKILL.md describing the procedure and when to use it.
Add the script under scripts/ and reference it.
Put the folder in the project's .claude/skills/ folder and commit it.
Ask the agent for a matching task and check that the skill loads.
recipes.example: A release-notes skill whose script collects merged pull requests and lets the agent draft the notes.

installation.why: An interpreter and packages for the script on each machine, plus the right skills folder.

usage.why: Ask for the task in plain language and review the result.

recipes.title: Fan-out review with a workflow
recipes.why: Hundreds of files can be checked by independent reviewers, and the team gets one merged result instead of a long chat.
recipes.what: A workflow script starts one subagent per item, collects the findings and returns a single result. The script holds the plan, so the main conversation stays small.
how: Describe the check and ask for a workflow.
Try it on one directory first to see the token use.
Approve the plan and watch the run in /workflows.
Save the run as a command if you want to repeat it.
recipes.example: Audit every route handler under src/routes/ for missing authentication checks.

installation.why: Nothing to install. The feature may have to be switched on.

usage.why: Scale, cost and permissions need judgement, and the findings need checking.

recipes.title: An agent that knows your tools and rules
recipes.why: The agent can work with your own systems and follows your team rules from the first message of every session.
recipes.what: The harness reads the instruction file at the start and calls the MCP server's tools when a task needs them.
how: Write the instruction file with the team rules.
Register the MCP server in the harness settings.
Choose which of its tools the agent may use.
Run a first task and review each permission prompt.
recipes.example: The agent looks up a ticket through an MCP server and follows the team's commit rules from the instruction file.

installation.why: The MCP entry and the permissions are set by hand, and the rules take a first draft.

usage.why: Ask in plain language and review what the agent did.

recipes.title: Semantic search inside PostgreSQL
recipes.why: Business data and its embeddings stay in one database, so there is one system to back up, secure and run.
recipes.what: pgvector adds vector columns, distance operators and approximate indexes to PostgreSQL. An application stores embeddings next to the rows and searches by similarity with SQL.
how: Run PostgreSQL 13 or later with pgvector installed.
Run CREATE EXTENSION vector; in the database.
Add a vector(N) column that fits your embedding model.
Insert embeddings and query with ORDER BY embedding <-> '[...]' LIMIT 5.
recipes.example: A support-ticket table gets an embedding column, and similar past tickets are found with one SQL query.

installation.why: A server, an extension and an embedding pipeline must be set up.

usage.why: Needs SQL, an embeddings model and index tuning.

recipes.title: Local semantic search in one file
recipes.why: A script or small app can search by meaning with no database server, and the whole index travels as one file.
recipes.what: sqlite-vec adds vec0 virtual tables to a SQLite connection. Vectors are stored in the database file and searched with a MATCH query ordered by distance.
how: Install the sqlite-vec binding for your language.
Enable extension loading and load the extension on the connection.
Create a vec0 virtual table and insert embeddings.
Query with MATCH and ORDER BY distance.
recipes.example: A command-line tool indexes meeting notes and returns the five notes closest to a question.

installation.why: The extension must match the platform and be loaded by hand. It is pre-v1.

usage.why: Needs embeddings from a model and tolerance for interface changes.
